lessons.title: Vowel Harmony
lessons.explanation: Turkish has vowel harmony: suffixes change their vowels to match the last vowel of the stem. There are two groups: back vowels (a, ı, o, u) and front vowels (e, i, ö, ü). A suffix with 'e' becomes 'a' after back vowels; a suffix with 'i' becomes 'ı', 'u', or 'ü' depending on the stem.
examples: ev + de = evde (in the house) — front vowel
araba + da = arabada (in the car) — back vowel
gel + iyor = geliyor (is coming) — front vowel
bak + ıyor = bakıyor (is looking) — back vowel
lessons.tip: Vowel harmony is the key to Turkish. Once you learn a suffix pattern, you just apply the matching vowel.

quiz.question: Turkish vowel harmony means that suffixes must match the __ of the stem.

lessons.title: SOV Order and Suffixes
lessons.explanation: Turkish is SOV (Subject-Object-Verb). The verb goes LAST. Turkish is agglutinative — many suffixes are stacked onto one word to express meaning. Example: evlerimizde = ev+ler+imiz+de = house+plural+our+in = 'in our houses'.
examples: Ben kitap okuyorum. (Ben = I, kitap = book, okuyorum = am reading)
O elma yiyor. (He/she is eating an apple.)
Biz okula gidiyoruz. (We are going to school.)
evlerimizde (in our houses) — 4 suffixes on one word
lessons.tip: In Turkish you can often express a whole English sentence with one heavily suffixed verb.

quiz.question: What is the word order of Turkish sentences?

lessons.title: Personal Suffixes on Verbs
lessons.explanation: Turkish verbs conjugate with personal suffixes added at the end (after tense suffixes). Suffixes: -(y)ım/im/um/üm (I), -sın/sin/sun/sün (you sg.), — (he/she/it has no suffix), -(y)ız/iz/uz/üz (we), -sınız/siniz/sunuz/sünüz (you pl./formal), -lar/ler (they).
examples: Ben gidiyorum. (I am going.) — gid+iyor+um
Sen gidiyorsun. (You are going.) — gid+iyor+sun
O gidiyor. (He/she is going.) — gid+iyor
Biz gidiyoruz. (We are going.) — gid+iyor+uz
lessons.tip: The subject pronoun is often omitted in Turkish because the verb suffix shows who is doing the action.

quiz.question: What suffix marks 1st person singular in Turkish present tense?

lessons.title: Cases — Locative, Dative, Ablative
lessons.explanation: Turkish nouns take case suffixes. Locative (-da/-de/-ta/-te): at/in/on. Dative (-(y)a/-(y)e): to/toward. Ablative (-dan/-den/-tan/-ten): from/away from. All follow vowel harmony.
examples: evde (at home) — locative
okula (to school) — dative
şehirden (from the city) — ablative
masada (on the table) — locative
İstanbul'a (to Istanbul) — dative
lessons.tip: The key cases to learn first: -de (in/at), -e (to), -den (from). They're enough for most basic conversations.

quiz.question: What does the Turkish suffix -da/-de express?

lessons.title: Tenses — Present Continuous and Simple
lessons.explanation: Turkish present continuous: verb stem + -iyor + personal suffix (with vowel harmony). Simple present (habitual/general truth): verb stem + -er/-ar/-ir/-ur (etc.) + personal suffix.
examples: Kitap okuyorum. (I am reading a book.) — -iyor
Her gün kitap okurum. (I read a book every day.) — -r (simple present)
Şimdi yiyor. (He/she is eating now.) — -iyor
Genellikle erken kalkarım. (I usually wake up early.) — -r
lessons.tip: Use -iyor for ongoing actions; use -r for habits, facts, and schedules.

quiz.question: Which suffix forms the present continuous in Turkish?

lessons.title: Postpositions and Case Interactions
lessons.explanation: Turkish postpositions come AFTER the noun (like Japanese). Some require a specific case: için (for) uses nominative, ile (with) uses nominative, göre (according to) uses dative, önce (before) uses ablative.
examples: Senim için (for you) — için + nominative
arkadaşımla (with my friend) — ile attached as suffix
sana göre (according to you) — göre + dative
yemekten önce (before the meal) — önce + ablative
lessons.tip: Learn postpositions together with their required case — 'için + nominative' as one unit.

quiz.question: What case does 'için' (for) require in Turkish?

lessons.title: Evidentiality — Direct vs. Reported Past
lessons.explanation: Turkish has two past tenses distinguished by whether you witnessed the event directly. Definite past (-di): you saw it happen. Inferential/reported past (-miş): you heard about it or inferred it.
examples: Dün geldi. (He came yesterday.) — -di, you witnessed this
Dün gelmiş. (He apparently came yesterday.) — -miş, you heard this
Çok uyumuşsun! (You've slept a lot!) — -miş, you inferred from evidence
Deprem oldu. (An earthquake happened.) — -di, reported as fact
lessons.tip: -miş is also used in fairy tales (like 'once upon a time') and when reporting hearsay.

quiz.question: Which Turkish past tense suffix marks events you didn't witness directly?
